paper_title: Measuring Mechanistic Uncertainty in Large Language Models via Causal Robustness

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in critical domains, where their susceptibility to hallucinations makes reliable and interpretable uncertainty quantification essential. We introduce the concept of mechanistic uncertainty, which characterizes uncertainty through the stability of the internal mechanisms supporting a model's response. We propose the causal robustness margin, defined as the minimum internal intervention required to deviate the model's output, and operationalize it using Jacobian Lens (Jlens) concept steering vectors. Across three open-source models and five question-answering datasets, we show incorrect and uncertain responses exhibit smaller margins, indicating greater sensitivity to internal interventions, and the causal robustness margin complements conventional output-based uncertainty methods. Finally, in a controlled knowledge injection experiment, correctly learned facts show increased margins after training, suggesting that causal robustness provides a mechanistically grounded signal of uncertainty.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes real-world settings, where confidently incorrect responses can have severe consequences (Kalai et al., 2026). Uncertainty quantification (UQ) asks how much confidence to place in an individual prediction, which is essential for building reliable and trustworthy systems, particularly in domains such as healthcare (Hager et al., 2024) and natural sciences (Chen et al., 2024). Many existing UQ methods, however, characterize uncertainty at the level of model outputs, using signals such as verbalized confidence (Xiong et al., 2024), sequence likelihood, entropy (Huang et al., 2025), semantic entropy (Kuhn et al., 2023), or self-consistency across multiple generations (Wang et al., 2023). While these approaches can indicate whether an answer appears uncertain, they pro1 vide limited insight into why that uncertainty arises within the model. Predictive uncertainty asks, how uncertain is the model about its prediction? However, it does not reveal whether the internal computations supporting response are stable or small perturbations to those computations would produce different answer. recent line of work explores LLM uncertainty through internal representations and computations utilizing tools from mechanistic interpretability (Olah, 2022; Meng et al., 2022). These studies investigate internal dispersion of activations (Brzezinka, 2026; Bu et al., 2026b; Srey et al., 2026), supervised uncertainty probes (Teplica et al., 2025; Bu et al., 2026a), and identifying uncertainty directions in representation space (Kumaran et al., 2026; Ferrando et al., 2025). We study complementary question: how robust is the internal computation supporting the models prediction? Rather than measuring uncertainty only from the output distribution, we ask whether it can be inferred from the robustness of the internal causal process that gives rise to the models response. Understanding and evaluating the robustness of models internal computations is crucial first step toward reliable uncertainty quantification, as uncertainty arising from data cannot be meaningfully assessed without model robustness (Ahdritz et al., 2024). In this paper, we introduce mechanistic perspective on uncertainty in LLMs, which we refer to as mechanistic uncertainty. Our central hypothesis is that LLMs own uncertainty can be characterized by the stability of the internal causal mechanism that produces models response. Motivated by this intuition, we propose the causal robustness margin, defined as the minimum magnitude of an intervention required to deviate the models response denoted as α. Our approach uses an analogous principle to notions of minimal perturbation in adversarial robustness (Szegedy et al., 2013; Madry et al., 2018) and counterfactual explanations (Wachter et al., 2017), where we seek minimal change to an input or representation that induces different model outcome. In our case, we intervene directly on intermediate representations and measure how strongly they must be perturbed before the generated response changes. recent mechanistic interpretability method, Jacobian Lens (Jlens) (Gurnee et al., 2026), makes this study possible. Jlens significantly improves upon classic methods such as logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) by linearly transporting intermediate activations through the downstream computation using average Jacobians, and allows for causal analysis of readouts and interventions in the direction of verbalizable concepts. We define our causal robustness margin through controlled Jlens interventions across three open-source models and five question answering datasets. We find that incorrect responses generally exhibit smaller causal robustness margins and that these margins complement output-based uncertainty measures. controlled knowledge injection experiment further shows increased margins for newly correct responses after training on knowledge sources for specific entities, linking successful learning to greater internal stability. Together, these findings support causal robustness as an intervention-based signal of uncertainty. An overview of the intuition for our method is shown in Fig. 1. Our main contributions are: We introduce the novel concept of mechanistic uncertainty as the causal fragility of an internal computation supporting response. We formalize the notion using the causal robustness margin, defined as the minimum intervention required to semantically deviate from the baseline response. We implement the causal robustness margin using the Jlens to steer toward or away from the representation of consensus tokens poised to be verbalized prior to generation. We perform experiments on five datasets and open-source LLMs and show that the causal robustness margin can predict response correctness, complements output-based uncertainty methods, and captures internal mechanism stability.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs. LLM uncertainty is commonly estimated from verbalized Figure 1: We perform different magnitudes of steering α (both positive and negative) along Jlens consensus token vectors to determine mechanistic uncertainty. Response flips at lower magnitude steers, as shown in the example, indicate high mechanistic uncertainty. We use mid to last layer activations due to informative verbalizable tokens, whereas earlier layers contain lot of noise. confidence (Xiong et al., 2024), predictive distributions, entropy (Huang et al., 2025), or sampled outputs (Wang et al., 2023). Verbalized confidence can be poorly calibrated (Zhao et al., 2026), while likelihood and entropy-based measures operate over lexical realizations and may not capture semantic equivalence. Semantic entropy addresses this by clustering sampled responses by meaning before computing uncertainty (Kuhn et al., 2023). In contrast, our work takes mechanistic and interventional approach to uncertainty quantification. Mechanistic Interpretability. Mechanistic interpretability aims to identify the internal representations and components responsible for model behavior (Olah, 2022) for capabilities such as indirect object identification and factual recall (Wang et al., 2022; Ferrando et al., 2025). Observational tools such as the logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) decode intermediate residual states into vocabulary distributions, while the Jacobian lens (Jlens) (Gurnee et al., 2026) significantly improves these readouts and allows interventions in the direction of verbalizable concepts. Interventional methods instead manipulate internal representations to test their causal role. These include steering along concept directions (Park et al., 2024; Ferrando et al., 2025), component ablations (Wang et al., 2022), causal tracing(Meng et al., 2022), and other circuit discovery techniques (Hanna et al., 2023; Conmy et al., 2023). Mechanistic Studies of Uncertainty in LLMs. Recent work has further examined mechanistic signatures of uncertainty: Kadavath et al. (2022) use 2 internal activations, such as P(IK) probes that predict whether model knows an answer; Teplica et al. (2025) identify overlap between uncertainty and factuality-related components using probederived signals; Bu et al. (2026a) use causal-tracing restoration probabilities as features for supervised uncertainty prediction; and Srey et al. (2026) predict correctness from layer-wise hidden-state variability. Sampling-free methods exploit internal dynamics directly, including semantic convergence across layers (Bu et al., 2026b) and geometric hidden-state trajectories (Wang et al., 2025). Finally, Kumaran et al. (2026) show that internal confidence representations can causally influence behaviors such as abstention. Despite this progress, most methods predict uncertainty from statistics dervied from internal features. In contrast, we study whether sensitivity to causal interventions provides an intrinsic measure of uncertainty, linking uncertainty to the models underlying computational mechanisms.

sections.title: 3 Background
sections.content: Jacobian Lens. Recently, Gurnee et al. (2026) proposed Jacobian Lens (JLens), mechanistic interpretability tool to explore the representations of LLMs, and discovered global workspace of concepts that model is poised to verbalize at any point in its processing. For each token in the models vocabulary, Jlens identifies vector representation that encodes the potential for the model to verbalize that token in the future. These Jlens vectors comprise subspace of the models representation space, coined J-space. Formally, Jlens characterizes an intermediate activation vector by its first order causal effect on the models outputs. For residual stream vector hℓ,t at layer ℓ, token t, perturbing the representation shifts the residual stream vectors at subsequent layers and token positions. sections.title: 4.1 Mechanistic Uncertainty
sections.content: An LLM generates responses through internal computations that transmit information across layers. These computations can be viewed as causal mechanisms where intervening on activations can change the response (Meng et al., 2022). These internal activation pathways should be stable across internal perturbations for given query. We precisely rely on this idea and hypothesize that uncertainty can be defined through the sensitivity of the causal mechanism generating the answer, and evaluate it at the activation level through semantically meaningful interventions. Complimentary to standard predictive uncertainty, which characterizes uncertainty in the models output prediction, we define mechanistic uncertainty as notion that captures the causal fragility of the internal computation supporting models response. Sensitivity to semantically meaningful intervention reveals how robustly model sustains an answer. If small interventions deviate the answers meaning, this may indicate the fragility of knowledge use or reasoning and indicates lower trust in the prediction. Predictive uncertainty asks how uncertain the model is about its prediction? Mechanistic uncertainty asks how stable is the internal computation that produces that prediction under controlled 3 causal interventions? We treat mechanistic uncertainty as distinct, interventional notion of uncertainty and investigate whether it correlates with and complements standard predictive uncertainty and response correctness. We mathematically define mechanistic uncertainty through the causal robustness margin, novel formulation of mechanistic uncertainty defined as the smallest intervention required to deviate an output as defined below. Definition 1 (Causal Robustness Margin) For let (x) denote the baseline some input x, output and (x) the output under specified intervention with magnitude m(I) from an arbitrary intervention set I. The causal robustness margin can be defined generally as R(x) = min II (cid:8)m(I) : (x) (x)(cid:9) , (4) where denotes deviation from the original output. Smaller margins indicate greater mechanistic uncertainty, while larger margins indicate greater robustness to the specified intervention.

sections.title: 4.2 Uncertainty via Causal Robustness
sections.content: Finding consensus in the workspace. Let fθ be an LLM and y0 = fθ(x) be the baseline answer generated by the LLM for given query x. Define = {ℓ1, ℓ2, . . . , ℓm} as the band of layers under study, where we intuitively choose the middle to late layers since they make up the workspace band consisting of the most relevant concepts processed by the model (Gurnee et al., 2026). The Jlens reveals that LLMs can often process different concepts in their workspace compared to their verbalized outputs. To study the consistency between the workspace and output space, we produce the token readouts for each layer in the band B. Intuitively, this measures the deviation of the models output from the original response under different causal intervention strengths, where the tendency to change answers from lower intervention strengths signals higher uncertainty.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: To understand what insights the causal robustness margin can provide with respect to uncertainty, we empirically study the following questions: Is causal robustness meaningfully associated with predictive reliability? Does causal robustness capture an additional dimension of uncertainty that cannot be inferred from model outputs alone? Does knowledge injection improve the stability of causal mechanisms through which the knowledge is expressed?

sections.title: 5.1 Setup
sections.content: Datasets and Models. We extensively evaluate our approach on several datasets, including opentext generation datasets TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 4 Figure 2: α plotted against accuracy. Binning is performed at each α value, and average accuracy is computed over each bin. The trend shows accuracy increasing with α. 2017), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022), PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023), and SciQ (Welbl et al., 2017), and one multiple-choice dataset MedQA (Jin et al., 2020). We experiment with three open-source LLMs that differ in architecture: Llama-3.1-8BInstruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-7BInstruct (Yang et al., 2024), and Gemma-3-12BInstruct (Gemma Team et al., 2025). Implementation Details. We use prefitted J-lens matrices1 to steer the final prompt-token activations across the last 10 layers, where readouts expose coherent verbalizable concepts. We search both positive and negative steering directions in increasing magnitude, with α {0.01, . . . , 0.50} using step size 0.01, stopping at the first semantic deviation from the baseline answer. The maximum magnitude is chosen empirically to capture flips in highly robust responses, and steering is normalized as in Eq. (8). For short-answer datasets, we evaluate correctness and answer flips using alias and exact matching. For TruthfulQA, we evaluate correctness with truthfulqa-truth-judge-llama2-7B2 and semantic deviation with Qwen3-32B.

We first measure the correlation between α and conventional output-based uncertainty metrics to see if mechanistic uncertainty shares information with output uncertainty, specifically self-consistency and mean token entropy. Self-consistency measures consistency across = 10 completions with temperature = 0.7. Mean token entropy averages the standard entropy over the token distribution at each step in generation. Across datasets and models, α correlates positively with selfconsistency and negatively with mean token entropy. Responses that are more robust and resistant to interventions generally show better agreement across sampled generations. 5.2.3 Acquiring domain-specific knowledge
stabilizes causal mechanisms
sections.content: Setup. We define knowledge injection in our setting as either introducing new knowledge or reinforcing existing knowledge. Several works have proposed methods for knowledge injection (Gekhman et al., 2024; Mecklenburg et al., 2024; Ovadia et al., 2025). We follow the paradigm from (Ovadia et al., 2025) and construct controlled entity-level supervised fine-tuning experiment using knowledge source (Wikipedia) and target dataset (PopQA). Since PopQA was introduced before the knowledge cutoff for all models evaluated, we do not claim the complete lack of such knowledge. Our main goal is to see if injecting knowledge or reinforcing existing knowledge improves causal robustness. We first construct knowledge instruct-response dataset using the procedure outlined in (Ovadia et al., 2025) (details in Appendix B). Starting from the base language model, we perform SFT on knowledge instruct-response pairs associated with target entities using the standard causal language modeling objective. We then evaluate the model on the same target dataset questions before and after SFT. We use questions from control set of entities that were unexposed to training for comparison. For each response, we compute α and define the overall change in causal robustness as = α post α pre (10) where positive values indicate that the response becomes more resistant to intervention after knowledge injection. We expect questions whose underlying entities were exposed during SFT should exhibit larger increases in α compared to matched questions involving unexposed entities, especially those questions that transition from incorrect to correct after training. Such result enables us to probe whether α responds to intervention on the parametric knowledge of the model and thereby shows less uncertainty and better stability. Results. The change for control entities is marginal for both models, which is consistent with the fact that those entities were excluded from training. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced mechanistic uncertainty as the fragility of the internal computation supporting an LLMs response. Using the JLens, we implement it through the causal robustness margin α, the minimum intervention to semantically deviate from the baseline response. Experiments show incorrect responses generally exhibit smaller margins, and α complements output-based uncertainty measures in predicting correctness. controlled knowledge injection experiment shows increased margins for newly correct responses. These findings support causal robustness as mechanistic uncertainty signal that connects to predictive reliability.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Since our focus in this work is mechanistic in nature, we evaluate limited set of open-source LLMs where we assume complete white-box access, including hidden states and token probabilities. Furthermore, the proposed causal robustness margin is based on Jlens-derived insights, including Jlens vector steer direction, layer bands, and normalization, which could vary for different models. Furthermore, the method requires sweeping several α values and apply steers across whole band, which can be computationally expensive. However, our main focus in this work is interpretability rather than efficiency. Despite these constraints, we show that the causal robustness margin is an uncertainty signal that consistently compliments conventional output-centric uncertainty methods and can reveal internal uncertainty behaviors in LLMs.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: This paper intends to advance the areas of interpretability and uncertainty quantification for language models and to make LLMs more reliable and trustworthy. All models used in this work are open-source. The datasets used are all publicly available.

sections.title: A Dataset details
sections.content: TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) TriviaQA is an open-domain factual question answering dataset collected from trivia and quiz league websites. Each question is associated with one or more semantically equivalent ground-truth answers. We randomly sample 1000 examples from the validation set for our experiments. SciQ (Welbl et al., 2017) SciQ is science question answering dataset consisting of crowdsourced multiple-choice questions covering topics such as physics, chemistry, and biology. Each question contains four answer choices with single correct answer. The dataset contains 13,679 questions from which we randomly sample 1000 for our experiment. We do not include the answer choices in the query for our experiments. TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022) TruthfulQA is question answering benchmark designed to evaluate whether language models produce truthful responses rather than reproduce common misconceptions or false beliefs. It contains 817 questions spanning 38 categories, including health, law, finance, and politics. Each question is accompanied by reference truthful and false answers, enabling evaluation of generated responses for both truthfulness and informativeness. We utilize the whole dataset for our experiment. MedQA (Jin et al., 2020). MedQA is medical question answering benchmark derived from professional medical licensing examinations. We use the English USMLE subset, which consists of 12,723 questions covering medical knowledge and clinical reasoning from which we randomly sample 1000 for our experiment. Each question is presented in multiple-choice format with single correct answer. PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023) PopQA is an entitycentric open-domain factual question answering dataset containing approximately 14,000 question answer pairs derived from Wikidata. We randomly sample 1000 examples for our experiment. The dataset associates entities with Wikipedia pageview statistics, providing measure of entity popularity. PopQA emphasizes long-tail and less popular entities for which language models typically exhibit weaker factual recall, making it useful

sections.title: Contextualization Prompt
sections.content: You are provided with factual statement about the following subject: {subject}. Specifically, the factual statement focuses on the following entity: {subject} within the context of the subject. The statement was taken out of the passage below and does not name its subject, so on its own it is unclear who or what it is about. Rewrite it so that it explicitly names {subject}, resolving pronouns and references such as he, she, it, the film or the musical, in way that fits naturally within the sentence. Keep every fact exactly as stated and add no other information. Return just the contextualized statement and nothing else. Statement: {fact} The passage about {subject}, for reference: {passage} Figure 4: Prompt for contextualizing with Qwen3-32B for studying the relationship between parametric knowledge and model confidence. Task-agnostic Instruction SFT details For our knowledge injection experiment on the PopQA dataset, we follow the steps outlined in the Knowledge-Instruct paper (Ovadia et al., 2025). The curated PopQA dataset consists of 1,935 longtail knowledge question and answer pairs, each with corresponding chunk of context retrieved from Wikipedia. We start with this context and build training dataset suitable for instruction tuning for knowledge injection with Mext as an extraction/summarization LLM (Qwen3-32B). Contextualization. First, we split the context into separate facts by treating each sentence as fact and ensure that the subject appears in each fact using Mext. Deduplication. Within each factual set, we remove redundant facts using Mext. Paraphrasing. For each fact, we generate set of 5 paraphrased variations using Mext. Instruction Conversion. We then convert each paraphrased fact into an instruction response pair (instruction, fact), where instruction is generic instruction template contextualized with the subject sampled from list of 25 templates specified in (Ovadia et al., 2025) including phrases such as Tell me fact about {entity}, What can you tell me about {entity}, etc.. 12 datasets, we can recover up to 10% - 20% of answers from the steer. We find that for many of these questions, the Jspace consensus reads the correct answers, but the model verbalizes an incorrect answer. This behavior illustrates that even for questions the model is uncertain about, factually correct answers may reside close in the Jspace. Mechanistic Uncertainty Correlation with other Uncertainty Signals. In Fig. 6, we include correlations with several additional uncertainty metrics such as max token probability, perplexity, energy (Liu et al., 2020), and semantic entropy. Max token probability is computed by taking the average of the maximum probability of the token distribution at each generated token. Semantic entropy (Kuhn et al., 2023) is computed over = 10 completions with temperature = 0.7, grouped into semantic clusters using an NLI model or string match, and computing entropy over the clusters. We find that α is positively correlated with max token probability and negatively correlated with perplexity, energy, and semantic entropy. As with selfconsistency and mean token entropy, the strongest correlations are often exhibited in the TriviaQA dataset. Intuitive Examples of Mechanistic Uncertainty. In Figs. 7 to 11, we include several examples from each dataset of fragile/incorrect and robust/correct responses to illustrate how the causal robustness margin captures uncertainty through mechanism stability.

sections.title: D Computational Resources
sections.content: We mainly utilize workstation with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 with 96GB RAM, and 2 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with 94GB RAM for our experiments.

sections.title: Paraphrasing Prompt
sections.content: Paraphrase the following factual statement {k} times. Each paraphrase must keep exactly the same meaning and every specific detail: do not change proper names, titles, dates, numbers or locations, and do not add or remove any information. Each paraphrase must be complete standalone sentence that names {subject}, and the paraphrases should differ from the original and from each other in wording and sentence structure. Return only JSON array of {k} strings and nothing else.
